## Chapter 28. Hepatitis
Acute viral hepatitis is presented as diffuse liver inflammation, beginning with a nonspecific viral prodrome followed by anorexia, nausea, and often fever or right upper quadrant pain (Chapter 28. Hepatitis — Acute Viral Hepatitis, p. 322). Jaundice often develops as other symptoms begin to resolve (Chapter 28. Hepatitis — Acute Viral Hepatitis, p. 322). Most cases resolve spontaneously, but some progress to chronic hepatitis, and occasionally to acute hepatic failure / fulminant hepatitis (Chapter 28. Hepatitis — Acute Viral Hepatitis, p. 322). Specific notes vary by virus: HCV may be asymptomatic during acute infection, with fluctuating severity (Chapter 28. Hepatitis — Chapter 28. Hepatitis, p. 324); acute HDV typically manifests as unusually severe acute HBV infection or an exacerbation in chronic HBV carriers (Chapter 28. Hepatitis — Characteristics of Hepatitis Viruses], p. 324). Diagnosis is by liver function tests — AST and ALT elevated out of proportion to alkaline phosphatase, usually with hyperbilirubinemia — and serologic tests to identify the virus (Chapter 28. Hepatitis — Acute Viral Hepatitis, p. 322; Chapter 28. Hepatitis — Diagnosis, p. 324). In the prodromal phase hepatitis mimics nonspecific viral illnesses and is difficult to diagnose, and is usually suspected only during the icteric phase (Chapter 28. Hepatitis — Diagnosis, p. 324). Treatment is usually supportive (Chapter 28. Hepatitis — Acute Viral Hepatitis, p. 322).

## Chapter 23. Approach to the Patient With Liver Disease
Common nonspecific symptoms in liver disorders include fatigue, anorexia, nausea and occasionally vomiting, while jaundice is described as the most specific symptom and is often accompanied by dark urine and light stools (Chapter 23. Approach to the Patient With Liver Disease — Evaluation, p. 276). Fever can develop in viral hepatitis (Chapter 23. Approach to the Patient With Liver Disease — Evaluation, p. 276), and right upper quadrant pain usually results from distention or inflammation of the liver capsule (Chapter 23. Approach to the Patient With Liver Disease — Evaluation, p. 276). Prodromal symptoms before jaundice, such as fever, malaise and myalgias, are listed among important associated symptoms in evaluating jaundice (Chapter 23. Approach to the Patient With Liver Disease — Evaluation, p. 282). Acute jaundice, particularly with a viral prodrome, in the young and healthy is noted to suggest acute viral hepatitis (Chapter 23. Approach to the Patient With Liver Disease — Key Points, p. 285). Symptoms may be attenuated in the elderly, e.g. abdominal pain may be mild or absent in acute viral hepatitis (Chapter 23. Approach to the Patient With Liver Disease — Geriatrics Essentials, p. 285).

## Chapter 263. Pregnancy Complicated by Disease
Acute viral hepatitis is described as the most common cause of jaundice during pregnancy, may predispose to preterm delivery but does not appear teratogenic, and is generally mild, while hepatitis E may be severe (Chapter 263. Pregnancy Complicated by Disease — Hepatic Disorders in Pregnancy, p. 2803).

## Chapter 149. Viruses
Viral hepatitis is listed among disorders caused by viruses affecting primarily the liver, transmitted by contact with infected blood or body secretions, or by the fecal-oral route for hepatitis A and E, with hepatitis D infecting only when hepatitis B is present (Chapter 149. Viruses — Ch. 28, p. 1557).

## Chapter 128. Transplantation
This chapter's passages mention viral hepatitis only in the context of liver transplantation, including recurrence of hepatitis B and C after transplantation and differential diagnosis of rejection (Chapter 128. Transplantation — Chapter 128. Transplantation, p. 1274).

Synthesis: The manual characterises acute viral hepatitis chiefly by a prodrome of anorexia, nausea, fever and right upper quadrant pain followed by jaundice as symptoms improve (Chapter 28. Hepatitis — Acute Viral Hepatitis, p. 322), with jaundice described as the most specific symptom among liver disorders (Chapter 23. Approach to the Patient With Liver Disease — Evaluation, p. 276).

## Title 28 — Judiciary and Judicial Procedure

Title 28 provides that district courts have original jurisdiction over all civil actions arising under the Constitution, laws, or treaties of the United States (28 U.S.C. § 1331). The surrounding provisions in the retrieved passages address distinct, specific bases of jurisdiction, e.g., actions against foreign states (28 U.S.C. § 1330), diversity and class-action jurisdiction (28 U.S.C. § 1332), bankruptcy cases (28 U.S.C. § 1334), patents and copyrights (28 U.S.C. § 1338), and suits by or against the United States (28 U.S.C. §§ 1345-1346), rather than the general federal-question basis stated in § 1331.

## Title 48 — Federal Acquisition Regulations System (CFR)

The retrieved Title 48 passages address federal contracting qualifications and procedures, not the general federal-question jurisdiction provision (e.g., 48 C.F.R. § 652.236-71; 48 C.F.R. § 652.237-73).

## Title 20 — Employees' Benefits (CFR)

The retrieved Title 20 passages address Social Security and related administrative hearing procedures and jurisdiction of administrative bodies, not the general federal-question jurisdiction provision (e.g., 20 C.F.R. § 404.944; 20 C.F.R. § 501.2).

## Title 29 — Labor (CFR)

The retrieved Title 29 passages address labor administrative review and related proceedings, not the general federal-question jurisdiction provision (e.g., 29 C.F.R. § 7.1; 29 C.F.R. § 9.34).

## Title 38 — Veterans’ Benefits

The retrieved Title 38 passages address veterans’ benefits, insurance suits, and review by the Federal Circuit, including exclusive Federal Circuit jurisdiction over certain challenges to the validity of statutes or regulations in that specific veterans’ system (38 U.S.C. § 7292), not the general federal-question jurisdiction provision.

Synthesis: The directly relevant passage is 28 U.S.C. § 1331, which states the federal-question basis for original district-court jurisdiction. Other retrieved passages address narrower jurisdictional or administrative contexts.
